quizzes.title: Week 1 Quiz
quizzes.description:
Week 1 Quiz
7th Grade ELA · A Midsummer Night's Dream · Week 1
16 points16 questions2 attemptsAbout 15 minutes
Before you move on
 

Confirm your Week 1 submissions before you move on:

☐Lesson 1 PDF
☐Lesson 2 PDF
☐Lesson 3 PDF
☐Lesson 4 PDF
☐This Week 1 Quiz

questions.text: Egeus brings a complaint against Lysander to Duke Theseus. What is Egeus's claim, the belief he wants the Duke to accept?

answers.text: That Demetrius has broken the law of Athens and should be punished by the Duke.
That Hermia has already secretly promised herself to Lysander in front of witnesses.
That as her father he may decide whom Hermia marries.
That Lysander should be sent away from Athens for good.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. "As she is mine I may dispose of her" (Shakespeare, 1.1). Everything else in his speech supports that belief.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Look for the belief underneath the whole speech, not the details he uses to prove it.

questions.text: Which of these is evidence Egeus offers to support his complaint?

answers.text: Lysander's rhymes, his songs at Hermia's window, and the love-tokens he gave her.
Demetrius's promise, made in front of the whole court, to marry Hermia at the new moon.
A letter Hermia wrote to Lysander and hid from her father.
A ruling the Duke made in an earlier case about another family.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Egeus lists what Lysander did, then calls it bewitching.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Egeus lists specific things Lysander did. What does he actually name?

questions.text: What does Egeus ask the Duke to do if Hermia will not obey?

answers.text: Forgive Hermia and let her choose freely.
Make Lysander apologize in front of the Duke and the whole court.
Make Hermia marry Demetrius or take a vow never to marry.
Make Hermia marry Demetrius or face death under the old law.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. Egeus asks for the "ancient privilege of Athens": marriage to Demetrius, or the old law's penalty. The vow never to marry is the Duke's own addition, in his ruling.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Read the end of Egeus's speech, from "I beg the ancient privilege of Athens". The choice of a vow comes later, from the Duke.

questions.text: Why does Lysander want to reach his widow aunt's house?

answers.text: She has agreed to speak to Egeus on Lysander's behalf and calm him down.
The law of Athens cannot follow them there.
Demetrius does not know the way there.
The Duke has ordered them to go there until the new moon.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. "The sharp Athenian law / Cannot pursue us" there (Shakespeare, 1.1), so they can marry.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Find the reason Lysander gives for that place in particular.

questions.text: After Hermia and Lysander tell Helena their plan, what does Helena decide to do?

answers.text: Keep the secret so that her friend Hermia can get away safely.
Warn Egeus at once so that he can stop his daughter.
Tell Demetrius, hoping to win his thanks.
Follow the couple to the wood without telling anyone at all.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. She will tell Demetrius of "fair Hermia's flight", though she knows the thanks will cost her dearly.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Think about whom Helena loves, and what she hopes telling him will win her.

questions.text: Hermia swears "by Cupid’s strongest bow, / By his best arrow with the golden head," (Shakespeare, 1.1). These lines are allusions. What is she swearing by?

answers.text: Figures from old Roman stories about love.
The laws of Athens that the Duke has just read out to her.
Her father's name and the honor of his house.
The gifts and love-tokens Lysander has given her.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Cupid, the god of love with his bow and arrows, comes from old Roman myth. An allusion points to a story the audience already knows.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Who is Cupid? Is he part of Athens's law, or part of an old story?

questions.text: Quince wants his company to rehearse in the palace wood, not in the city. Why?

answers.text: The wood is closer to the Duke's palace, where they will perform.
Snug needs room to practise roaring like a lion.
The Duke has ordered every play to rehearse outside the town.
In the city they would be followed and their plans found out.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. Quince fears that "if we meet in the city, we shall be dogg’d with company, and our devices known" (Shakespeare, 1.2).
questions.feedback_incorrect: Read Quince's last long speech. What does he fear would happen in the city?

questions.text: Theseus tells Hermia, "To you your father should be as a god;" (Shakespeare, 1.1). What does he mean?

answers.text: Egeus is a priest, so Hermia must listen to him at the temple.
A daughter should obey her father completely.
Egeus is the most powerful man in all of Athens, more powerful than the Duke.
Hermia should pray for her father every night.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Theseus says her father made her, like a figure pressed in wax, and has power over her.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Read the next lines: what does Theseus say her father did, and what power does he say Egeus has?

questions.text:
What tense is the verb gathers?

Example sentence: The court gathers here every morning.

answers.text: past
present
future
past perfect

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Gathers tells something that happens regularly now: present tense.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Is this already done, happening now, or still to come?

questions.text: Which sentence is in the past tense?

answers.text: She will explain her plan to the court tomorrow.
They are leaving the city tonight with their friends.
He remembered every word of the ruling.
The door opens slowly.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Remembered shows an action already finished: past tense.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Look for the verb that tells something already done.

questions.text:
In this sentence, had set is an example of which tense?

Example sentence: By the time Egeus arrived, the Duke had already set his wedding day.

answers.text: future tense
present tense
future perfect
past perfect

questions.feedback_correct: Right. Had plus a past verb marks the earlier of two past events: the wedding day was set before Egeus came.
questions.feedback_incorrect: When had comes before a past verb, it marks something already done before another past event.

answers.text: He raised his hand; the room went quiet.
She argued; because she believed she was right.
The list included; songs, tokens, and letters.
She wanted; to be heard.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Both sides are complete thoughts, so the semicolon can join them.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A semicolon needs a complete thought on both sides. Check each side.

answers.text: She needed: more time to decide before she gave her answer.
The teacher explained: the rule carefully and slowly to the class.
Bottom wanted three parts: Pyramus, Thisbe, and the lion.
He ran: as fast as he could.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. A complete thought comes first, then the list that explains it.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A colon follows a complete thought and opens a list or an explanation. Which one has a complete thought before the colon?

questions.text:
What does the colon do in this sentence?

Example sentence: He had only one hope, one plan, one chance: to be believed.

answers.text: It joins two complete sentences.
It opens what his hope, plan and chance were.
It shows that a list of action verbs is coming next in the sentence.
It takes the place of a question mark.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. What comes after the colon names the one thing the sentence has been building toward.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Is "to be believed" a complete sentence? What does it do for the words before the colon?

questions.text:
What is had doing in this sentence?

Example sentence: Hermia had promised to meet Lysander before Helena arrived.

answers.text: It is a linking verb showing a state of being.
It is an adverb telling when the promise happened.
It is the subject noun of the sentence.
It is a helping verb forming the past perfect.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. Had + promised shows the promise came first, before Helena arrived.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Had sits in front of the main verb promised. What job does a word in that spot do?

questions.text: Lysander's line "But either it was different in blood—" (Shakespeare, 1.1) ends with a dash. Why?

answers.text: Hermia cuts in before he can finish.
A list of three things follows it.
It joins two complete thoughts into one sentence.
It marks the end of a question he asks Hermia.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Hermia answers "O cross!" before he finishes, and he picks up again with "Or else". A dash can show a speaker breaking off.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Read the next two speeches. Who speaks right after the dash, and how does Lysander go on?
